body.html: Cells constantly adjust to stay in homeostasis. Under stress they can adapt (reversible change in size, number, phenotype or metabolism); if the stress is mild/transient this is reversible cell injury, but if severe/progressive it becomes irreversible injury and cell death (necrosis or apoptosis). Adaptations can be physiological (normal hormonal stimuli, e.g. breast enlargement) or pathological (the cell's way of escaping injury). Five patterns: hyperplasia, hypertrophy, atrophy, metaplasia, dysplasia.

Atrophy: shrinkage in cell size from loss of substance, usually from decreased activity — less protein synthesis, energy shortage, and increased proteasome/lysosome breakdown; reversible if normal conditions return. Physiological causes: normal ageing (sarcopenia, brain volume loss), menopause/andropause (endometrial, vaginal, testicular atrophy), thymic involution after puberty. Pathological causes: malnutrition/starvation, denervation (loss of trophic nerve signals), chronic ischaemia (atherosclerosis → fibrosis), pressure (compression by a tumour or amyloid), disuse/immobilisation, and autoimmune villous atrophy in coeliac disease. Hypoplasia = congenital underdevelopment of a tissue/organ (e.g. pulmonary hypoplasia); aplasia/agenesis = the organ is wholly or largely absent from a developmental defect.

Hypertrophy: increase in cell SIZE (and function), no change in cell number; occurs in terminally differentiated cells that cannot divide (cardiac, nerve, skeletal muscle = "pure" hypertrophy) or together with hyperplasia in cells that can still divide (epithelial, smooth muscle = "mixed"). Causes: increased demand (cardiac hypertrophy from hypertension/aortic stenosis, weightlifting, compensatory renal hypertrophy) or hormonal stimulation (TSH → thyroid, oestrogen → pregnant uterus and breast). Function eventually plateaus and can fail (e.g. hypertensive heart failure).

Hyperplasia: increase in cell NUMBER (only possible if cells can still divide), increasing organ volume without architectural distortion; driven by growth factors (EGF, PDGF, TGF-β, VEGF) and hormones (oestrogen, androgens, TSH, prolactin), and by stem-cell activation after injury. Physiological: pregnancy-related breast/uterine hyperplasia, compensatory liver regrowth after resection. Pathological: chronic irritation (calluses), excess hormones (benign prostatic hyperplasia from DHT; multinodular goitre). Generally benign but chronic hyperplasia can be a precursor to cancer (e.g. endometrial hyperplasia → carcinoma).

FeatureHyperplasiaHypertrophyNeoplasia
Cell numberIncreasedUnchangedIncreased (abnormal)
Cell sizeNormalIncreasedVariable
ControlRegulatedRegulatedUncontrolled

Reversible replacement of one mature differentiated cell type by another, better suited to withstand the stress — normal architecture, abnormal location/cell type. Caused by chronic irritation: acid/bile reflux (Barrett's oesophagus: squamous → columnar/intestinal-type), smoking (bronchial columnar → squamous), H. pylori (gastric → intestinal metaplasia), HPV (cervical squamous metaplasia). Mechanism: reprogramming of stem cells by cytokines/growth factors in the tissue microenvironment; reverses when the stimulus stops. Clinically important because it is precancerous: intestinal metaplasia → gastric adenocarcinoma; Barrett's oesophagus → dysplasia → oesophageal adenocarcinoma; squamous metaplasia of the bronchus → squamous cell carcinoma.

Dysplasia is disordered cellular development/growth: loss of uniformity of individual cells and of their architectural orientation, with variation in cell size and shape, enlarged/hyperchromatic nuclei and loss of normal polarity. It typically arises in a background of chronic metaplasia or hyperplasia and carries an increased risk of malignant transformation. Mild dysplasia can be reversible if the cause is removed; severe dysplasia is a step on the pathway toward carcinoma in situ and invasive cancer (as in Barrett's oesophagus: intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma).

Carcinogenesis (oncogenesis, tumorigenesis) is non-lethal genetic damage acquired from environmental agents (chemicals, radiation, viruses) or inherited in the germ line. A tumour is the clonal expansion of a single damaged progenitor cell (tumours are monoclonal) whose alterations give growth and survival advantages. It is a multistep process: initiation → promotion → progression, with sub-clones acquiring more aggressive behaviour over time (e.g. colorectal cancer: APC loss (5q) → DNA hypomethylation → RAS mutation (12p) → loss of 18q suppressor → p53 loss (17p)).

Phases G1 (growth), S (DNA replication), G2 (preparation), M (mitosis). Checkpoints: G1/S (DNA integrity, nutrients), G2/M (complete replication), metaphase/anaphase (chromosome attachment). Driven by cyclins and CDKs; braked by p53 (halts the cycle on DNA damage) and RB (controls G1→S by blocking cyclin E transcription). Cancer cells have dysregulated checkpoints, uncontrolled proliferation, ignore stop signals and often disable apoptosis. CDK inhibitors (palbociclib) are therapeutic targets.

Chemicals: initiators cause DNA damage — direct-acting need no metabolic conversion (alkylating agents, anticancer drugs such as cyclophosphamide, acylating agents); indirect-acting require activation by cytochrome P-450 into an ultimate carcinogen (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons like benzopyrene, aromatic amines/azo dyes like β-naphthylamine and benzidine); others: aflatoxin B1, nitrosamines, vinyl chloride, nickel, chromium, insecticides, PCBs. Promoters are not carcinogenic alone but make initiated cells proliferate. Radiation: UV, X-rays, nuclear fission, radionuclides. Microbial agents: DNA viruses — HPV (E6 binds p53, E7 binds RB; types 16 and 18 → cervical, anogenital, oropharyngeal squamous carcinoma), EBV (LMP1 activates NF-κB/JAK-STAT and BCL2 → Burkitt lymphoma), HHV8 (Kaposi sarcoma), HBV (hepatocellular carcinoma); RNA virus HTLV-1 (TAX → T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma); bacterium H. pylori (chronic inflammation, proliferation, ROS, CagA → gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma).

Four classes: proto-oncogenes (growth-promoting), tumour suppressor genes (growth-inhibiting), apoptosis regulators, DNA-repair genes. Oncogenes are mutated/overexpressed proto-oncogenes, dominant (one allele suffices), gain of function (KRAS, EGFR). Tumour suppressors need loss of function: governors brake proliferation (RB) and guardians control genomic damage — TP53, "guardian of the genome", arrests the cycle or triggers apoptosis; guardian mutations accelerate other mutations. Four alteration types: base substitutions (EGFR L858R in lung, BRAF V600E in melanoma), indels (EGFR exon 19 deletion; 13q14/RB deletion in retinoblastoma; 17p deletion loses p53), copy-number changes (HER2 amplification in 20% of breast cancers → trastuzumab/pertuzumab; NMYC amplification in 25–30% of neuroblastomas, poor prognosis; CDKN2A loss removes p16/p14), rearrangements/fusions (ALK, RET, NTRK, FGFR fusions; t(8;14) MYC in Burkitt; t(14;18) BCL2 in follicular lymphoma; t(9;22) Philadelphia BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase in CML; t(11;22) EWS-FLI1 in Ewing sarcoma). Epigenetics: reversible heritable expression changes without mutation — histone modification and DNA methylation; promoter hypermethylation silences suppressors (p16/INK4a widely, p14/ARF in colon and gastric cancer).

1. Self-sufficiency in growth signals: autocrine loops (glioblastoma/PDGF), stromal growth factors, receptor overexpression or mutation (HER2), self-activated downstream signalling, deregulated transcription factors. 2. Insensitivity to growth inhibitors: loss of RB (or HPV E7 binding RB). 3. Evasion of cell death: BCL2 overexpression via t(14;18) makes follicular lymphoma indolent. 4. Limitless replication: reactivation of telomerase overcomes telomere-driven senescence. 5. Sustained angiogenesis: hypoxia → HIF-1α → VEGF; new vessels are leaky and haphazard; needed for growth and metastasis; targeted by bevacizumab. 6. Invasion and metastasis: local invasion → intravasation → transit → extravasation → micro- then macrometastases. ECM invasion: loosening of cells (E-cadherin loss) → proteolysis of basement membrane (MMPs, cathepsin D, urokinase) → altered attachment (integrins) → migration. Cells travel singly or as emboli with platelets; organ tropism via adhesion molecules and chemokines (breast cancer CXCR4/CCR7). 7. Immune evasion: tumour antigens (mutated RAS, BCR-ABL, p53; overexpressed tyrosinase/MART; cancer-testis antigens MAGE/BAGE; viral E6/E7; oncofetal CEA/AFP) are presented on MHC I to CD8+ CTLs — the dominant antitumour mechanism, especially for virus-associated tumours; NK cells are the first line without prior sensitisation; M1 macrophages (IFN-γ, ROS, TNF); humoral therapy such as anti-CD20 rituximab.

Precursor (precancerous) lesions: benign lesions predisposing to cancer — surely (genetic: familial adenomatous polyposis, xeroderma pigmentosum) or possibly (acquired: colonic adenoma, ulcerative colitis, bladder papilloma, gastric atrophy, cirrhosis). Four stages: 1. local (organ of origin: dysplasia, carcinoma in situ), 2. locoregional (invasive carcinoma infiltrating adjacent organs and vessels), 3. generalisation (tumour emboli), 4. metastasis (secondary tumours). Routes: lymphatic (preferred by carcinomas; nodal spread is prognostic), haematogenous (preferred by sarcomas, also renal cell and follicular thyroid carcinoma), transcoelomic (peritoneal, pleural, pericardial, subarachnoid spaces — ovarian carcinoma to the liver surface).

Two types of cell death: necrosis and apoptosis. They differ in mechanism, morphology and role in disease. Neither is autolysis, the post-mortem digestion of a cell by its own enzymes. Cell death precedes the visible morphological changes (ultrastructural, then microscopic, then gross).

Cell death with severe membrane damage: lysosomal enzymes leak into the cytoplasm and digest the cell; contents leak into the extracellular space and trigger inflammation. Always pathological, no recovery. Causes: anoxia/ischaemia, physical agents, chemicals and drugs, infections, immune reactions, nutritional imbalance. Morphology: cytoplasm becomes more eosinophilic and glassy (denatured proteins, lost RNA and glycogen); nucleus shows pyknosis (shrinkage), karyorrhexis (fragmentation) and karyolysis (dissolution), disappearing within 1–2 days. Tissue necrosis = a group of cells dying under the same stress (e.g. myocardial infarction after coronary thrombosis, oesophageal necrosis after caustic ingestion).

Coagulative: frequent; architecture preserved for days, proteolysis blocked, anucleate ghost cells; typical of infarcts in all solid organs except the brain. Liquefactive: bacterial/fungal infection; leukocyte enzymes digest tissue into a viscous liquid. Caseous: tuberculosis; friable yellow-white, amorphous granular debris with architecture obliterated, bordered by a granuloma. Gangrenous: a limb that has lost its blood supply, coagulative necrosis of multiple tissue layers, often with anaerobic bacteria. Fat necrosis: acute pancreatitis (released lipases) or breast trauma (cytosteatonecrosis). Fibrinoid: immune complexes plus leaked fibrin deposited in artery walls (e.g. polyarteritis nodosa).

Programmed "cellular suicide": the cell activates enzymes that degrade its own DNA and proteins, fragments into apoptotic bodies with an intact plasma membrane, and is rapidly phagocytosed — no inflammation. Physiological: embryogenesis, involution of hormone-dependent tissue (endometrium, lactating breast after weaning), turnover of proliferating populations (intestinal crypts), removal of neutrophils after inflammation and lymphocytes after an immune response, killing of virus-infected or tumour cells by cytotoxic T cells. Pathological: DNA damage (radiation, chemotherapy), misfolded proteins, some viral infections (adenovirus, HIV).

FeatureNecrosisApoptosis
Cell sizeEnlargedReduced
NucleusPyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysisFragmentation into nucleosome-size pieces
Plasma membraneDisruptedIntact, altered lipid orientation
ContentsDigested, leak outIntact, in apoptotic bodies
InflammationYesNo
RoleAlways pathologicalOften physiological; pathological after DNA/protein damage

Apoptosis is executed by caspases (proteases): activators (2, 8, 9, 10) switch on executioners (3, 6, 7), which drive DNA fragmentation, chromatin condensation and membrane changes. Two pathways: the mitochondrial (intrinsic) pathway, the most frequent, triggered from inside the cell and controlled by the balance of pro-apoptotic (Bax/Bak, BH3 proteins) and anti-apoptotic (BCL-2) proteins, leading to caspase 9; and the death receptor (extrinsic) pathway, triggered from outside (Fas/FasL on activated T cells) via caspase 8. Clinically: BCL-2 overexpression in follicular lymphoma blocks apoptosis; p53 arrests the cycle at G1/S for DNA repair and activates Bax if damage is beyond repair — p53 mutations are found in many cancers. Therapies: anti-BCL2 drugs, chemo/radiotherapy (DNA damage → apoptosis).

Cells live in a steady state (homeostasis). Excess stress forces a new steady state (adaptation); if the cell cannot adapt it is injured. Mild injury is reversible (the cell repairs and heals); severe injury is irreversible and ends in cell death (necrosis or apoptosis).

Genetic causes and acquired causes: physical agents (mechanical trauma, heat/cold, electricity, UV and ionising radiation, rapid pressure change); chemicals and drugs (cyanide, arsenic, mercury, strong acids/alkalis, pollutants, pesticides, high-concentration oxygen, hypertonic glucose/salt, alcohol, narcotics, therapeutic drugs); microbial agents (bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites); immunologic agents (hypersensitivity, anaphylaxis, autoimmunity — immunity is a double-edged sword); ageing (senescence impairs replication and repair). Psychogenic diseases show no specific morphological change, but addiction, alcoholism and smoking cause organic disease.

Outcome depends on the type, duration and severity of the agent, the type and adaptability of the target cell (skeletal muscle tolerates hypoxia a long time; cardiac muscle is irreversibly injured after >20 min), and the intracellular events involved. Ischaemia/hypoxia is the commonest form: no oxygen → mitochondria cannot make ATP → membrane pumps fail → calcium accumulates in the cytoplasm, which poisons mitochondria, damages proteins and DNA, and activates enzymes that destroy membranes. The second major pathway is free radicals (from inflammation, radiation, chemicals, toxins) that damage the cell membrane. Reversible injury shows membrane blebs, swollen ER and mitochondria, and myelin figures; irreversible injury is marked by nuclear changes and then death.

Hydropic change (cloudy swelling, vacuolar degeneration): water accumulates in the cytoplasm; the earliest and commonest form, fully reversible; organ swollen with a bulging opaque cut surface; swollen cells with clear vacuoles. Hyaline change: glassy, homogeneous eosinophilic proteinaceous material — intracellular (hyaline droplets in proximal tubules in proteinuria, Zenker's degeneration in typhoid, Mallory bodies in alcoholic liver, Russell bodies in plasma cells) or extracellular (leiomyoma, old scars, hyaline arteriolosclerosis in hypertension/diabetes). Mucoid change: excess mucin — epithelial mucin is PAS-positive (catarrhal inflammation, cystic fibrosis, mucinous tumours) while connective-tissue (myxoid) mucin is PAS-negative but colloidal-iron positive (fibroadenoma, myxoedema); both stain with Alcian blue. Fatty change: neutral fat within parenchymal cells, especially the liver.

DegenerationWhat accumulatesClassic examples
HydropicWaterKidney tubules, liver, heart (earliest, commonest)
HyalineGlassy proteinMallory bodies, Russell bodies, Zenker, arteriolosclerosis
MucoidMucinCystic fibrosis, mucinous tumours, myxoedema
FattyNeutral fatLiver, heart, kidney

Cell death is the state of irreversible injury: necrosis (the cell bursts, releases contents and attracts inflammation) or apoptosis (quiet, programmed death). Neither is autolysis, the post-mortem digestion of cells by their own enzymes. Changes following local death include gangrene and calcification.

Inflammation is the response of living, vascularised tissue to injury, taking place in the vascular connective tissue. It aims to eliminate or isolate the aggressor and repair the tissue. Acute inflammation is the immediate, intense vasculo-exudative response to a short, often brutal aggression, dominated by neutrophils, lasting days to weeks and usually resolving. Celsus's four signs: rubor, tumor, calor, dolor (redness, swelling, heat, pain), plus loss of function (Virchow). Biology: leukocytosis, raised ESR and CRP. Causes: exogenous (infection, physical/chemical agents, foreign bodies) or endogenous (ischaemic necrosis, dysregulated immunity, autoimmunity).

Phagocytes: macrophages (monoblast → monocyte → tissue histiocyte; cytokine release, bacterial lysis, phagocytosis) and granulocytes (neutrophils: chemotaxis, lysosomal proteases, phagocytosis; eosinophils: parasites and allergy; basophils: histamine/serotonin). Mast cells near vessels release histamine. Lymphocytes (T/CD3, B/CD20, NK) are uncommon in acute inflammation. Fibroblasts/myofibroblasts make matrix; endothelial cells control permeability and angiogenesis. Plasma mediators: complement (~20 proteins, lysis and opsonisation), kinins (bradykinin: smooth-muscle contraction, permeability, pain), coagulation/fibrinolysis (factor XII → fibrin). Cellular mediators: histamine (mast cells/basophils; first released, acts in 1 min for ~10 min; vasodilatation + permeability), serotonin (platelets), PAF, nitric oxide (endothelium/macrophages), arachidonic-acid metabolites, and cytokines — pro-inflammatory IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6; anti-inflammatory IL-4, IL-10, IL-13.

MediatorOriginMain effects
HistamineMast cells, basophilsFirst released; vasodilatation, permeability
SerotoninPlateletsPermeability
PAFLeukocytes, mast cellsVasodilatation, permeability, adhesion, chemotaxis
Nitric oxideEndothelium, macrophagesSmooth-muscle relaxation
BradykininPlasma kinin systemContraction, permeability, pain

IL-4, IL-10, IL-13LymphocytesAnti-inflammatory

Initiated by cell activation (mast cells +++) and histamine release. Congestion: arteriolar then capillary vasodilatation and slowing of flow → redness and heat. Inflammatory oedema: endothelial retraction opens intercellular gaps, raised hydrostatic and permeability → protein-rich exudate → swelling and pain. The oedema dilutes toxins, brings immunoglobulins/complement (opsonins) and fibrinogen (fibrin barrier), and slows flow to favour diapedesis — but can be harmful by volume or site (laryngeal, cerebral, acute pulmonary oedema). Leukocyte diapedesis: slowing of flow → margination → rolling and adhesion (selectins) → passage between endothelial cells with basement-membrane degradation → migration by chemotaxis along a gradient (bacterial products, necrotic tissue, complement, arachidonic-acid metabolites). Neutrophils first (6–24 h), then monocytes (24–48 h); lymphocytes may come first in viral infection, eosinophils in some hypersensitivity.

The inflammatory granuloma is the set of cells at the site: neutrophils early, then macrophages/histiocytes and lymphocytes. Phagocytosis: recognition (opsonins — complement or antibodies — or Toll-like receptors) → ingestion (pseudopods → phagosome) → digestion (phagosome + lysosome = phagolysosome, low pH, hydrolytic enzymes). Leukocyte-function defects cause recurrent, severe infections. Debridement cleans the site: internal (macrophages phagocytose neutrophils, lymphatic/venous drainage of oedema) or external (spontaneous fistulisation or surgical incision). Without complete debridement the process becomes chronic. Systemic effects: fever (TNF/IL-1 → hypothalamic prostaglandins), acute-phase proteins (CRP, fibrinogen, SAA via IL-6 on the liver), leukocytosis (CSFs), and in severe sepsis septic shock (high TNF).

Outcome depends on the agent, damage severity, host status and tissue regenerative capacity (labile tissues renew constantly — marrow, epithelia; stable tissues regain proliferation when injured — liver, kidney, pancreas; permanent tissues cannot regenerate — myocardium, neurons). Resolution: short-lived mediators, anti-inflammatory signals (IL-1ra, IL-4, IL-10, IL-11, TGF-β), lipoxins, resolvins and protectins. Repair needs complete debridement and good vascularisation: granulation tissue appears at 1–4 days (neo-vessels by angiogenesis under VEGF/angiopoietin; fibroblasts/myofibroblasts driven by TGF-β, PDGF, FGF, IGF; matrix rich in type III collagen), then remodels to type I collagen with myofibroblast contraction → fibrous scar, or restitution ad integrum; the brain repairs by astrocytic gliosis. Epithelial regeneration starts at the edges from basal cells. Abnormalities: fibrous scar without adnexa, metaplastic regeneration, pyogenic granuloma (botriomycoma), keloid. Complications: persistent vascular phenomena (congestive, oedematous, haemorrhagic e.g. Waterhouse-Friderichsen, fibrinous e.g. pericarditis) or cellular phenomena (suppurative: pus/pyocytes → pustule, abscess, phlegmon with streptococcal hyaluronidase, empyema; necrotising e.g. gangrenous cholecystitis). If the agent persists → chronic inflammation: mononuclear cells and fibrosis, months to years, no spontaneous recovery.

Suppurative formDefinition
PustulePus within or beneath the epidermis
AbscessLocalised pus cavity in a solid organ (elastase, collagenase)
PhlegmonDiffuse spread, no collection; streptococcal hyaluronidase
EmpyemaPus in a natural cavity (pleura)

Pathology (Greek: study of diseases) is the branch of medicine studying structural and functional changes in tissues and organs caused by disease. It sits at the interface of basic sciences (anatomy, physiology, biochemistry) and clinical sciences (surgery, oncology, internal medicine, etc.), providing the scientific foundation for diagnosis and treatment.

Anatomical pathology is practised only by pathologist physicians (unlike general medical analyses, which biologists — physicians or pharmacists — can also perform).

Pathology studies visible modifications (lesions) caused by disease, at three levels: macroscopic (naked eye/magnifying glass), microscopic tissue level (pathological histology) and microscopic cellular level (pathological cytology). A lesion is any structural damage or abnormal change caused by disease; an elementary lesion affects one structure, a lesional complex combines several. Lesions may be malformative, inflammatory/immune, circulatory (e.g. atherosclerosis), or neoplastic (e.g. adenocarcinoma).

Traditionally split into general pathology (basic mechanisms: cell injury, inflammation/repair, haemodynamic disorders, growth disorders/neoplasia) and systematic pathology (how these mechanisms play out in each organ system). Branches include histopathology, cytopathology, molecular pathology and forensic pathology; human pathology (patient tissue) is distinguished from experimental pathology (animal models, cell culture).

title: Disease process: aetiology, pathogenesis, lesion, clinic
subject: subj:pathanat

body.html:
Four linked aspects explain a disease: aetiology (the cause — "why"; known cause = primary, unknown = idiopathic; genetic or acquired — infectious, nutritional, chemical, physical), pathogenesis (the mechanism — "how" the cause produces disease), morphological changes/lesions (the resulting structural alterations, gross or microscopic), and clinical manifestations (the symptoms/signs, course and prognosis that follow from those structural changes).

TermMeaningExample
AetiologyThe causeHPV in cervical cancer; idiopathic if unknown
PathogenesisThe mechanismIncubation period of an infection
LesionStructural changeCirrhotic nodules, granuloma
Clinical manifestationsSymptoms and signsJaundice, cough, fever

Anatomical pathology reasons by analogy: comparing normal histology with pathological tissue, then correlating findings with clinical data and imaging/biology (the anatomo-clinical correlation). Tools: macroscopic examination, optical (photonic) microscopy, plus immunohistochemistry, molecular biology and (rarely) electron microscopy. Roles of pathology: diagnostic (anatomo-clinical diagnosis), prognostic (e.g. pTNM staging, margin status in cancer), therapeutic response (regression/persistence/worsening of lesions), and research (treatment efficacy).

Oncology (onkos = mass) is the study and treatment of tumours. A tumour is an excessive cellular proliferation forming a tissue mass that resembles the normal tissue of origin, persists, grows, and escapes normal growth and differentiation controls. In molecular terms a neoplasm is a disorder of cell growth caused by acquired mutations in a single cell and its clonal progeny. "Cancer" (Latin, crab) refers to malignant tumours. Tumour tissue = tumour cells + stroma (supporting connective tissue and vessels). Cancer is the second cause of death worldwide after cardiovascular disease; commonest cancers are prostate (men) and breast (women), while lung cancer kills the most in both.

Environmental factors: infections (HPV, HBV), smoking (lung, oral cavity, pancreas), alcohol (liver, oral cavity, breast), diet and obesity, oestrogen exposure (breast, endometrium), carcinogens (UV → skin, arsenic, asbestos → mesothelioma, benzene → leukaemia, radon → lung). Hereditary cancer: familial cancers, inherited cancer syndromes, defective DNA-repair syndromes. Prevention: avoid carcinogens, vaccination (HBV, HPV); screening detects pre-invasive stages (Pap smear, BRCA testing). Normal stem cells self-renew, differentiate or undergo apoptosis under homeostatic control; aggression alters genetic information and disrupts control → excess proliferation and/or decreased death. Possible sequence: benign → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive.

Excessive abnormal proliferation (swelling); persistent growth after the stimulus fades (biological autonomy); clonality (mono-, oligo- or polyclonal); variable differentiation (resemblance to the parent cell); a multi-step accumulation of genetic errors. Hallmarks acquired: self-sufficiency in growth signals, insensitivity to growth inhibitors, evasion of cell death and limitless replication (immortality), invasion and metastasis, angiogenesis, metabolic reprogramming (aerobic glycolysis), immune evasion. The two unique properties of cancer cells are local invasion and metastasis.

Benign: well circumscribed, encapsulated, pushing borders, homogeneous cut surface; well differentiated with few normal mitoses and no cytonuclear abnormality; slow local growth, no relapse, good prognosis (can still cause morbidity by site). Malignant: poorly circumscribed, non-encapsulated, infiltrates and destroys surrounding tissue, heterogeneous (necrosis, haemorrhage); variably or undifferentiated, frequent abnormal mitoses, cytonuclear abnormalities (hyperchromatism, multinucleation, pleomorphism); rapid growth, invasion, relapse, metastasis. Metastasis is the only indisputable criterion of malignancy: benign tumours cannot metastasise. There is a continuum (tumour progression: colorectal adenoma → low- then high-grade dysplasia → adenocarcinoma), plus locally aggressive tumours with benign morphology (desmoid tumour/fibromatosis) and low-malignancy tumours (basal cell carcinoma). Anaplasia = complete undifferentiation (pleomorphism, hyperchromatic bizarre nuclei, many atypical mitoses, architectural anarchy), almost always malignant. Dysplasia = intra-epithelial architectural and cytological atypia (hypercellularity, enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei, high N/C ratio, loss of polarity, mitoses), graded mild/moderate/severe, then carcinoma in situ when dysplastic cells fill the whole epithelium without crossing the basement membrane.

FeatureBenignMalignant
BordersWell circumscribed, capsule, pushingPoorly circumscribed, infiltrative
Cut surfaceHomogeneousHeterogeneous: necrosis, haemorrhage
DifferentiationWell differentiatedVariable to undifferentiated
MitosesFew, normalFrequent, abnormal
GrowthSlow, local, no relapseRapid, invasive, relapse
MetastasisNeverPossible

Malignant and poorly differentiated tumours grow faster; growth depends on blood supply, hormones and aggressive sub-clones. Growth fraction (% dividing cells) is high early and in leukaemias/lymphomas/small-cell lung cancer (chemo/radiosensitive) and low in breast/colon cancer (debulking). Half of patients have metastases at diagnosis. Grading (microscope) rates how abnormal the tumour looks — e.g. breast: tubules + pleomorphism + mitoses each scored 1–3, total 3–5 low grade (>95% 5-year survival), 6–7 intermediate (80%), 8–9 high (60%). Staging (imaging + pTNM) says how far it has spread: T size/extent (Tis in situ, T1–4), N regional nodes (N0–N3), M distant metastasis (M0/M1); used for solid tumours, less for lymphomas/leukaemias. Pseudotumours are not neoplasms: inflammatory (chronic inflammation, foreign body, pyogenic granuloma, keloid, pseudotumoral tuberculosis), hormonal (goitre, gynaecomastia, adrenal or endometrial hyperplasia), developmental (heterotopia: e.g. pancreatic tissue in the gastric antrum).

Benign: cell type + "-oma" — adenoma (glandular epithelium), papilloma (squamous, finger-like), polyp (projects into a lumen; adenomatous polyp if glandular), cystadenoma (cystic), fibroma, lipoma, chondroma, osteoma, rhabdomyoma, leiomyoma, haemangioma, lymphangioma; adenomas are usually small, solitary and encapsulated. Malignant: carcinoma for epithelium (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell/epidermoid carcinoma; variants: signet-ring, papillary; basal cell carcinoma) and sarcoma for mesenchyme (fibrosarcoma, liposarcoma, chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, angiosarcoma). Exceptions that are malignant despite "-oma": melanoma, lymphoma (and leukaemia), glioma. Special categories: mixed tumours (adenosquamous carcinoma, carcinosarcoma, pleomorphic adenoma, fibroadenoma), teratomas (from pluripotent cells of the three germ layers; ovary and testis, midline extra-gonadal sites; 95% mature/benign, mostly ovarian; 5% immature/malignant, mostly testicular), and blastomas (malignant childhood tumours from organ blastema: nephroblastoma/Wilms, retinoblastoma, medulloblastoma, hepatoblastoma; chondroblastoma and osteoblastoma are benign exceptions).

Anatomic pathology studies two sample types: cytological (cells only: FNA, Pap smear, body fluids) and histological (cells and tissue: biopsies, surgical specimens, autopsy). Histopathology and cytopathology differ in sampling and processing but both feed the pathological report.

Cytological specimens: spontaneously emitted fluids, scraping/brushing/swabbing (Pap smear), needle aspiration of a fluid or of an organ/tumour (FNAC), blind or imaging-guided.

Tissue samples: biopsy (percutaneous with a cutting needle/trocar, or surgical, incisional or excisional), surgical specimen (organ or part removed during surgery), and autopsy (forensic when death may be criminal, or clinical/academic to find the medical cause). Biopsies must be numerous, large enough, centred on the lesion, well handled (avoid crush/electrocoagulation artefact) and labelled.

Standard workflow: fresh specimen → fixation (usually 10% formalin, which penetrates rapidly and does not over-harden tissue; 1–few hours for biopsies, 24–72h for surgical specimens, volume at least 10–15× tissue bulk) → dehydration (increasing alcohol baths, removes the fixative) → clearing → wax infiltration/impregnation (paraffin replaces water, hardens tissue for cutting) → embedding (paraffin block) → section cutting on a microtome, 3–5 microns thick → staining, standard being H&E (haematoxylin stains nuclei blue/acidic, eosin stains cytoplasm pink/basic) → mounting → microscopic examination.

Special stains highlight specific components: PAS (glycogen, mucin), Alcian blue (mucin), Fontana (melanin), Perls (haemosiderin/iron), Von Kossa (calcification), Masson's trichrome (fibrosis/collagen), Congo red (amyloid — apple-green birefringence under polarised light).

Immunohistochemistry (IHC) detects an antigen with a specific antibody linked to an enzyme or fluorochrome, producing a visible coloured reaction.

Molecular biology (PCR, DNA microarrays, sequencing) detects RNA/DNA — viral genomes (e.g. EBV), tumour diagnosis, prognosis (e.g. N-Myc in neuroblastoma), and therapeutic targets (e.g. EGFR mutations guiding anti-EGFR therapy).

Frozen section: rapid intraoperative diagnosis, tissue fixed by freezing and cut on a cryostat. Advantage: speed; disadvantage: lower section quality than paraffin, so it must always be confirmed on permanent (paraffin) sections. Used to identify an unknown process, evaluate margins, or detect metastases — not indicated when the result has no immediate impact on the operation, or when the tissue is scarce and better kept for permanent processing.

The pathological report is signed and is the key document guiding treatment. Storage: residual tissue fragments about 1 month in formalin, then incinerated; paraffin blocks and slides at least 10 years (lifelong in paediatric pathology); a tumour bank keeps fresh frozen samples at −80°C with consent for molecular studies.

Vessel walls have three constituents — endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, extracellular matrix (elastin, collagen, glycosaminoglycans) — arranged in three layers: intima (single endothelial layer, bounded by the internal elastic lamina), media (smooth muscle, bounded by the external elastic lamina) and adventitia (connective tissue with nerves and vasa vasorum). Arteries: large elastic (aorta, media rich in elastin), medium muscular (coronary, renal), small arteries and arterioles. Capillaries have endothelium but no media, slow flow, ideal for exchange. Veins: larger lumens, thinner disorganised walls, valves, easily compressed or invaded by tumour. Lymphatics: thin endothelial channels draining interstitial fluid and inflammatory cells — a pathway for bacteria and tumour spread. Leukocyte extravasation and vascular leakage occur in post-capillary venules.

Haemodynamics studies blood flow and its forces: blood pressure (systolic/diastolic), cardiac output (stroke volume × heart rate), vascular resistance (diameter, viscosity); regulated neurally (baroreceptors, autonomic system), hormonally (RAAS, ADH) and locally (autoregulation, NO, endothelin). Fluid exchange is governed by Starling's law: capillary hydrostatic pressure (from the heart's pumping) pushes fluid out, higher at the arteriolar end; plasma oncotic pressure (albumin) pulls fluid back, dominant at the venular end; interstitial pressures oppose. The small residual excess is drained by lymphatics. Too much pushing (heart failure) or too little pulling (liver disease, malnutrition) → oedema.

Transudate: low protein (<3 g/dL), few cells, clear, specific gravity <1.012–1.016; from a hydrostatic/oncotic imbalance without inflammation (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome). Exudate: high protein (>3 g/dL), many cells, cloudy, specific gravity >1.020; from increased vascular permeability due to inflammation, infection or injury (pneumonia, pleuritis, cancer).

Oedema (Greek oideima, swelling) is abnormal accumulation of interstitial fluid; in body cavities it is an effusion. It becomes evident when interstitial fluid increases by 2.5–3 L. Water is 60% of body weight: two-thirds intracellular, one-third extracellular (intravascular, interstitial, transcellular). Five major causes: 1. increased hydrostatic pressure (heart failure, DVT, venous obstruction); 2. reduced plasma oncotic pressure (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, malnutrition); 3. increased permeability/inflammation (endothelial injury by toxins, histamine, anoxia, burns → protein leak); 4. lymphatic obstruction (radical mastectomy, filariasis, tumour, lymphangitis → lymphoedema); 5. sodium and water retention (renal failure, hyperaldosteronism: hypovolaemia → renin/aldosterone/ADH → Na and water retention).

By distribution: localised (trauma, cellulitis, insect bites, DVT) or generalised/anasarca (heart, kidney, liver failure, severe protein deficiency). By composition: transudative (cardiac) or exudative (inflammatory). By physical character: pitting (indentation persists after pressure — water retention: heart, kidney, liver disease, DVT, varicose veins, pregnancy) or non-pitting (lymphoedema, lipoedema, myxoedema). Inflammatory oedema: mediators histamine, bradykinin, TNF-α, IL-1; vasodilatation, protein leak, neutrophil/macrophage infiltration, overwhelmed lymphatics → protein-rich exudate; swelling, redness, heat, pain; microscopy shows dilated vessels, neutrophils, fibrin, pink exudate (cellulitis, abscess). Haemodynamic (non-inflammatory) oedema: transudate from altered Starling forces — cardiogenic, renal, hepatic. Major sites: peripheral (legs, ankles: venous insufficiency, heart failure, kidney disease, lymphatic obstruction), pulmonary (left heart failure, ARDS, toxin inhalation, high altitude; dyspnoea, pink frothy sputum; may add pleural effusion), cerebral (trauma, stroke, infection, tumour, hyponatraemia; narrow sulci, flat gyri; headache, seizures, coma), macular (diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion; blurred vision) and lymphoedema (post-surgery/radiation, congenital; heavy limb, skin thickening).
